y-m-57-01.title: Is this correspondence a function or not?
y-m-57-01.topic: Meaning of a function: a correspondence with one result for each input
y-m-57-01.goal: Judge correspondences by the standard 'one result for each input', show with examples you build yourself that different inputs can have the same result and still be a function, and say how to fix a correspondence that is not a function so that it becomes one.
y-m-57-01.material:
When there is a correspondence (a rule), we want to look at what result comes out for one input. There are four correspondences below.
(가) Match each student in a class to that student's attendance number. (Each student already has one attendance number.)
(나) Match each positive integer x to the positive divisors of x. (Example: for 6, they are 1, 2, 3, 6)
(다) Match each integer x to the square of x.
(라) Match each real number x that is 0 or more to 'the real number y whose square equals x'.
y-m-57-01.thinking.0: Write out all the results for each input under the rule of the correspondence and judge
y-m-57-01.thinking.1: Build a function in which different inputs have the same result
y-m-57-01.thinking.2: Fix a correspondence that is not a function by changing its conditions so that it becomes one
y-m-57-01.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-01.prereq.1: The meaning of an element of a set and the word correspondence (middle-school level)
y-m-57-01.prereq.2: Putting a value into an expression to find the result
y-m-57-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the correspondences that are functions. (Function: a correspondence in which a result is determined for each possible input value)
y-m-57-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each correspondence, pick one input and write down all the results that come out.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark separately and compare the cases where the inputs differ but the result is the same, and the cases where one input has several results.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.r.a: This judgment counted, one by one, how many results (numbers) each input (student) has.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.o.b: (나) positive integer x → positive divisors of x
y-m-57-01.s.s1.r.b: Count how many results come out for the input 6. The standard is whether there is even one input with several results.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.r.c: This judgment separated whether different inputs (for example 2 and −2) are allowed to have the same result from the standard of how many results each input has.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.o.d: (라) real number x of 0 or more → y whose square is x
y-m-57-01.s.s1.r.d: For the input 4, write down all the real numbers y whose square is 4. The standard is counting how many there are.
y-m-57-01.s.s1.explain: The standard for a function is 'does one input give only one result'. (가) is a function because each student has one number, and (다) is a function because each integer has one square. It is fine that 2 and −2 both give 4 in (다). (나) is not a function because 6 gives 1, 2, 3, 6, and (라) is not a function because 4 gives 2 and −2.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.prompt: Consider a function f whose domain is {1, 2, 3} and whose codomain is {1, 2, 3, 4}. Make 3 different functions whose range has exactly 2 elements. (p = f(1), q = f(2), r = f(3))
y-m-57-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how many pairs among the three values f(1), f(2), f(3) must be equal to get two different kinds of values.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.hint.1: First choose the two inputs that will have the same value, and give the remaining input a different value.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All three values are inside the codomain {1, 2, 3, 4}.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.fail.c1: f(1), f(2), f(3) must each be one of 1, 2, 3, 4.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.fail.c2: You can only use elements of the codomain. Decimals are not in the codomain.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of different values that came out is exactly 2.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.fail.c3: There are not 2 different values. Check that the three values are not all the same or all different.
y-m-57-01.s.s2.explain: A range with 2 elements means that two of the three inputs have the same result. For example, f(1)=f(2)=1, f(3)=2 is also a function. There are 36 such functions in all. A function may have different inputs with the same result, but one input has only one result.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.prompt: How can you fix the rule of correspondence (라) to make it a function? Write the fixed rule and the reason that fixing it that way works.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write all the y that satisfy the condition when x=4.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what condition you could add to keep only one of those values.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your fixed rule, did you check yourself that an input like 4 gives only one result?
y-m-57-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the 'reason' connected to how many values corresponded to 4?
y-m-57-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether a different method from yours (for example, allowing only 0 or less) is also possible?
y-m-57-01.s.s3.model.0: I fix it so that only y of 0 or more is matched (the square root). Originally, when x=4, y had two values, 2 and −2, but if I limit it to 0 or more, only one result is left.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.model.1: I allow only non-negative values of y so that each input has one result. The problem was that 2 and −2 both came out at x=4.
y-m-57-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that expresses the way of limiting the range differently

y-m-57-02.title: Examining the statement 'if it is steeper, the slope is larger'
y-m-57-02.topic: Slope of a linear function: sign and steepness
y-m-57-02.goal: Know that 'steeper' and 'larger slope' do not always mean the same thing, find and fix the wrong line in a situation comparing slopes with different signs, and build a counterexample.
y-m-57-02.material: The graphs of the two linear functions y=2x and y=−3x are drawn on the same coordinate plane. The graph of y=2x goes up to the right, and the graph of y=−3x goes down to the right. The slope is 'the change in y when x increases by 1'. Below is a passage in which a student compared the two slopes.
y-m-57-02.thinking.0: Find the error by splitting the lines of the solution into facts and generalizations
y-m-57-02.thinking.1: Build a counterexample yourself where the generalization breaks
y-m-57-02.thinking.2: State the conditions under which the generalization holds
y-m-57-02.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-02.prereq.1: The meaning that in a linear function y=ax+b, the change in y when x increases by 1 is the slope a
y-m-57-02.prereq.2: Comparing the size of positive and negative numbers on a number line
y-m-57-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in this passage that contains a wrong claim. (Lines that follow from that claim can also be wrong.)
y-m-57-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into 'a fact read from the graph or equation' or 'a claim made from a rule'.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.hint.1: Place −3 and 2 on a number line and compare which one is further right with the steepness of each graph.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.line.0: For y=2x, when x increases by 1, y increases by 2.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.line.1: For y=−3x, when x increases by 1, y decreases by 3.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.line.2: The graph that is steeper has the larger slope.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.line.3: The graph of y=−3x is steeper, so the slope of y=−3x is larger.
y-m-57-02.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are facts read from the graph. Line 3, 'the steeper one has the larger slope', is the generalization, and it does not hold. Steepness compares the absolute values of the slopes (3 and 2), while the size of a slope, including its sign, compares −3 and 2. Line 4 is just the result of using line 3, and for line 5, −3 is to the left of 2 on the number line, so −3<2.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different linear functions y=ax+b that are steeper than y=2x but have a smaller slope. The y-intercept (b) must be 1.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.hint.0: First rewrite 'steeper' using the absolute value of the slope, and find the range on the number line that satisfies it together with 'the slope is smaller'.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.hint.1: Once you choose a candidate a, check the two conditions separately.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.ok.c2: It is steeper than y=2x (the absolute value of the slope is greater than 2).
y-m-57-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The steepness of the graph is not greater than that of y=2x.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The slope is not less than 2.
y-m-57-02.s.s2.explain: To be steeper, the absolute value of the slope must be greater than 2, and the slope must be less than 2, so a must be less than −2. Examples: y=−3x+1, y=−5x+1, y=−2.5x+1. a=3 has a larger slope too, so it is not a counterexample.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.prompt: Now write separately the cases where 'the graph is steeper' and 'the slope is larger' mean the same thing and the cases where they do not.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the order of steepness with the order of slopes when both slopes are positive, such as 2 and 5.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare in the same way the case where both are negative, such as −2 and −5.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check the case where they mean the same thing with two specific slopes?
y-m-57-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the other case to the counterexample made earlier?
y-m-57-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the case where the slope is 0?
y-m-57-02.s.s3.model.0: When both slopes are positive, the steeper one also has the larger slope. But when a negative is mixed in, steepness is compared by absolute value, so it can differ from comparing the size of the slopes.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.model.1: If both are lines going up to the right, the steeper one has the larger slope. If one is a line going down, compare steepness by absolute value, and compare slopes by looking at the sign too.
y-m-57-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer written with a focus on the negative side

y-m-57-03.title: The area of a vegetable garden when the fence length is fixed
y-m-57-03.topic: Maximum of a quadratic function and the allowed range of the variable
y-m-57-03.goal: Check with a table where the maximum of an area written as a quadratic expression occurs, judge for yourself that the position of the maximum can change when a new condition changes the range of the variable, and build solutions inside the range yourself.
y-m-57-03.material: You want to make a rectangular vegetable garden using one side of a wall. No fence goes on the wall side, and you use all of the 20 m of fence on the other three sides. If the two sides perpendicular to the wall each have length x m, then the side parallel to the wall is (20−2x) m. So the area of the garden is x(20−2x) m², and here 0<x<10.
y-m-57-03.thinking.0: Predict where the maximum is using a table
y-m-57-03.thinking.1: Revise your judgment by reflecting how a new condition changes the range of the variable
y-m-57-03.thinking.2: Find values that satisfy two conditions at the same time
y-m-57-03.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-03.prereq.1: Putting values into an expression containing a letter and calculating
y-m-57-03.prereq.3: Reading the range of values that satisfy an inequality
y-m-57-03.s.s1.prompt: At each step, look at the new information and choose your judgment about the x that makes the area largest.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put in x as 1, 2, 3, ... one at a time and calculate the area.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write the new condition as an inequality in x and first decide the possible range of x.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.info: As x gets larger, the sides perpendicular to the wall get longer, but the side parallel to the wall, (20−2x), gets shorter. You have not calculated any values yet.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: How does the area change as you make x larger from 0 toward 10?
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.after: When one side gets longer, the other side gets shorter, so you cannot decide from the effect of one side alone. 'b' is an estimate and 'd' is the judgment to check with a table. Let's check with a table.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It gets larger at first, then gets smaller from some point
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It gets smaller at first, then gets larger again
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You cannot say before calculating the values
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the table, what would you judge about the x that gives the largest area?
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The table has equal values on the left and right of 5 (4 and 6 give 48, 3 and 7 give 42). So 5 is the biggest candidate. If you rewrite the expression as −2(x−5)²+50, you can confirm that even for decimal x, 50 at 5 is the maximum.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I judge that it is largest when x=5 (among the integer values in the table, 5 is the maximum too)
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I judge that it is largest when x=4
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I judge that it is largest when x=6
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is near x=5, but it is too early to say for certain before checking decimal values
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: the wall where you will put this garden is only 8 m long. The side parallel to the wall, (20−2x), cannot be more than 8 m.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, among the possible x, how would you judge the value that gives the largest area?
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.2.after: From 20−2x≤8, x must be at least 6. If x=5, the parallel side is 10 m, which is longer than the wall, so it is impossible. For x≥6, the larger x is, the smaller the area, so 48 at x=6 is the maximum. The vertex of the expression (x=5) can be outside the possible range.
y-m-57-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The condition changed, so it cannot be decided
y-m-57-03.s.s1.reflect: When a new condition appears, it is not that your earlier judgment (x=5) was wrong; the 'possible range of x' changed, so the position of the maximum can change. Say which information changed your judgment, or whether you could have left it as it was.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.prompt: Under the condition that the wall is 8 m long, find 3 different values of x for which the area is 46 m² or more. (x can be a decimal.)
y-m-57-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the range of x from the wall condition, and test values only inside it.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find the area at x=6, then increase x a little at a time and see how the area changes.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.ok.c1: x is greater than 0 and less than 10.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be greater than 0 and less than 10.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The side parallel to the wall is 8 m or less.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The side parallel to the wall, (20−2x), is more than 8 m.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The area is 46 m² or more.
y-m-57-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The area is less than 46 m².
y-m-57-03.s.s2.explain: From the wall condition, x≥6, and from the area condition x(20−2x)≥46, x is about 6.41 or less. So values within 6≤x≤6.41 are the answer. For x=6.5 the area is 45.5, which is not enough.

y-m-57-04.title: To know the height of a ramp
y-m-57-04.topic: Trigonometric ratios: similarity of right triangles and length information
y-m-57-04.goal: Judge what information is enough to fix the height of a right triangle as one value, and confirm with examples you build yourself that if the angle is the same, the ratios of the sides are the same even when the lengths differ.
y-m-57-04.material: You want to put a straight ramp from level ground up to the entrance of a building. The bottom end of the ramp touches the ground and the top end touches the entrance floor, and the entrance is at a vertical height of h m above the ground. (The ground and the entrance floor are level, and the ramp, the vertical height and the horizontal distance on the ground form a right triangle.) Below are the sets of information the designer wrote down. Every 'angle' is 'the angle the ramp makes with the ground', and in this task we use sine (sin) 30° = 1/2 (= height ÷ hypotenuse).
y-m-57-04.thinking.1: Recognize that the angle alone does not fix the size
y-m-57-04.thinking.2: Build examples of similar right triangles yourself
y-m-57-04.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-04.prereq.1: Middle-school level understanding of the relationships among the sides of a right triangle
y-m-57-04.prereq.2: The meaning that the ratios of corresponding sides of similar figures are equal
y-m-57-04.prereq.3: The note that the sine of 30° is 1/2 (given within this task)
y-m-57-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the sets for which that information alone fixes the entrance height h as one value.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each set, count and write the number of 'known values' and 'unknown values'.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.hint.1: Picture two right triangles with the same angle but different sizes, and check whether the set tells the two triangles apart.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.o.a: Ramp length 10 m, horizontal distance 6 m from the bottom end of the ramp to the building
y-m-57-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment asks whether, when two sides of a right triangle are given, the remaining side is fixed as one value.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.o.b: The angle the ramp makes with the ground is 30°, the angle the ramp makes with the building wall is 60°
y-m-57-04.s.s1.r.b: The sum of the two angles is 90°, so it says the same information twice. There can be as many similar triangles of different sizes as you like.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.o.c: The fact that the ramp length is 4 m longer than the horizontal distance
y-m-57-04.s.s1.r.c: Even if there is one relationship between lengths, if there are two unknown values (the horizontal distance and the height), several triangles are possible. Count the number of relationships and the number of unknown values.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.o.d: Ramp length 10 m, the angle the ramp makes with the ground is 30°
y-m-57-04.s.s1.r.d: This judgment asks whether, with one angle and one side, the remaining sides are fixed by the ratio of similarity.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.o.e: The statement 'the ramp is gentle', horizontal distance 6 m
y-m-57-04.s.s1.r.e: 'Gentle' is not a value. Check whether it is information fixed by numbers.
y-m-57-04.s.s1.explain: a: The hypotenuse is 10 and one side is 6, so the other side (the height) is fixed as one value (8 m). d: The angle is 30°, so height ÷ hypotenuse is 1/2, and the hypotenuse is 10, so the height is 5 m. b says the same information about the two angles twice, so it cannot fix the size, c has two unknown values but only one relationship, and e is a description, not numbers. You need to know at least one length to fix the size.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.prompt: You want to put in more ramps that make the same angle with the ground (the same degree of slope). The first ramp has a horizontal distance of 4 m and a height of 3 m. Make 3 different new ramps with a horizontal distance of b m and a height of h m. (b and h are positive integers)
y-m-57-04.s.s2.hint.0: Express the relationship between the height and the horizontal distance of the first ramp as 'how many times'.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what the height must be to keep the same shape when the horizontal distance is made 2 times and 3 times as large.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.ok.c1: b and h are positive integers.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.fail.c1: b and h must be positive integers.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Height ÷ horizontal distance is the same as for the first ramp (3÷4).
y-m-57-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Height ÷ horizontal distance is not the same as 3÷4.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.ok.c3: It is a new ramp, not the first ramp.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.fail.c3: A horizontal distance of 4 m is the first ramp.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.explain: Right triangles with the same angle are similar figures, so the ratios of corresponding sides are equal. The first ramp has a hypotenuse of 5 m and height ÷ hypotenuse is 3/5. For the ramps you made, (8,6) and (12,9), the hypotenuses are different, 10 and 15, but height ÷ hypotenuse is the same 3/5.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.prompt: When the angle is the same, what does not change even though the lengths change, and why can you say so? Write it.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: For the two ramps you made, calculate the height divided by the horizontal distance for each.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Place the calculated values side by side and tell apart what changed from what stayed the same.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate height ÷ hypotenuse yourself for the two ramps you made?
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason 'similarity' with your calculation results?
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.model.0: A ratio such as height ÷ hypotenuse does not change. Right triangles with the same angle are similar figures, so the ratios of corresponding sides are equal.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.model.1: The sin value is constant. They are similar triangles that differ only in size, so the ratio of lengths stays the same.
y-m-57-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: A model answer written in trigonometric terms

y-m-57-05.title: Places that are the same distance from two base stations
y-m-57-05.topic: Coordinate plane: points that are the same distance from two points
y-m-57-05.goal: Know that the midpoint is not the only point that is the same distance from two points, build several different such points, and explain what shape they line up in.
y-m-57-05.material: On a coordinate plane (one grid unit is 1 km) there are base stations A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). You want to set up a temporary antenna at a point P(x, y). The distance between the points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is 'the positive square root of (x₁−x₂)²+(y₁−y₂)²'. The midpoint of two points is the point whose x-coordinate and y-coordinate are the averages of the two points' x-coordinates and y-coordinates. The midpoint of the two base stations A and B is M(4, 6).
y-m-57-05.thinking.0: Examine whether one familiar answer (the midpoint) is enough
y-m-57-05.thinking.1: Build several points that satisfy the condition
y-m-57-05.thinking.2: Generalize the rule of the points into a figure
y-m-57-05.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-05.prereq.1: Writing the position of a point as (x, y) on a coordinate plane
y-m-57-05.prereq.2: The meaning of the distance between two points and the midpoint (explained within this task)
y-m-57-05.prereq.3: Calculating with numbers that are not integers (decimals)
y-m-57-05.s.s1.prompt: How many points P are there that are the same distance from A and B?
y-m-57-05.s.s1.hint.0: Starting from the midpoint M, test one other point to see whether it satisfies PA=PB.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one point, calculate PA² and PB² each, and compare.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.r.a: It is true that the midpoint is such a point. But you must examine whether it is the only one. Compare the two distances of a point moved a little sideways from the midpoint.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.r.b: If you pictured the two points where two circles with fixed radii meet, that is a case where the distance values are fixed. Here the two distances only need to be equal to each other, and their value is not fixed.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment looks for and tests candidates besides the midpoint.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.o.d: It cannot be known from the coordinates alone
y-m-57-05.s.s1.r.d: The coordinates of A and B are given, so you can calculate and compare the distances. You can test yourself whether a certain point satisfies the condition.
y-m-57-05.s.s1.explain: The midpoint M(4, 6) satisfies PA=PB, but there are other points. For example, (8, 3) has the square of the distance to A equal to 7²+1²=50 and to B equal to 1²+7²=50, so they are equal. There are infinitely many such points on a line.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different points P(x, y) that satisfy PA=PB. Leave out the midpoint M, and P must be in the first quadrant (x>0, y>0). (Decimals are fine.)
y-m-57-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose x, then solve for what y must be so that the squares of the two distances are equal.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.hint.1: Place the points you found side by side and compare how much y changes when x changes.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.ok.c1: P is in the first quadrant.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must both be greater than 0.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The distance to A and the distance to B are equal.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance to A and the distance to B are not equal.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.fail.c3: You already know the midpoint M. Find another point.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.explain: If PA=PB, squaring both sides gives 3x+4y=36. All points of this line in the first quadrant are answers. Examples: (8, 3), (2, 7.5), (6, 4.5). This line passes through M(4, 6) and is perpendicular to AB.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what shape you think the points you found would make if plotted on the coordinate plane, with your reason for thinking so.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Roughly plot the three points you found on the coordinate plane and picture the shape they line up in.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare whether the midpoint M is on the same line as those points.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you pick two of the points you found and check whether the slopes are the same?
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether the midpoint is on the same line?
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the other possibility of a circle shape?
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.model.0: I think they are all on one line. It is the line that passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to AB, and you can see the rule that when x increases, y decreases at a constant rate.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.model.1: The points line up in a straight line. Like (8, 3), (6, 4.5), (2, 7.5), when x goes down by 2, y goes up by 1.5, and it passes through the midpoint.
y-m-57-05.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: A model answer written with the coordinate rule of the points found

y-m-57-06.title: What is 'typical' for the number of visitors?
y-m-57-06.topic: Representative values of data: how the mean and the median are used
y-m-57-06.goal: Look at how the mean and the median change when one very large value is mixed into the data, and judge that which value to use depends on what you want to do (the purpose), and say it with your own example.
y-m-57-06.material: A town library records the number of visitors (people) each day. The visitor numbers are used to decide the number of staff on duty and the amount of information materials to prepare. The record of the first 6 days is given in the steps below, and then the record of the 7th day is added.
y-m-57-06.thinking.0: Check your judgment when data is added
y-m-57-06.thinking.1: Find the standard (the purpose) for choosing a representative value
y-m-57-06.thinking.2: Build situations yourself where the mean fits and where the median fits
y-m-57-06.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-06.prereq.1: The meaning of the mean (sum of the data ÷ number of data) and the median (the middle value when placed in order of size)
y-m-57-06.s.s1.prompt: At each step, look at the new information and choose your judgment.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, arrange the data in order of size and calculate the middle value and the mean yourself.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write separately wanting to know the 'typical day' and wanting to know the 'total', and compare them.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Number of visitors (people) in the first 6 days: 40, 42, 45, 41, 43, 44. (The mean is 42.5 people, and when placed in order of size, the median, which is the average of the middle two values 42 and 43, is also 42.5 people)
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you described the number of visitors on a 'typical day' at this library with one value, what would be suitable?
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.after: The values are gathered between 40 and 45, so it is enough to say about 42.5 people. Now the record of the 7th day is added.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The mean and the median are the same, so this is data for which the conclusion is the same whichever you use.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The maximum is the busiest day, not a typical day.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There are only 6 data values, so you cannot say any value
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even with little data, if the values are gathered together you can make an estimate. Saying it is uncertain is different from saying you can say nothing.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 40 people (based on the least busy day)
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The minimum is the quietest day. It does not tell you the typical day.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.info: On the 7th day a town festival was held and there were 300 visitors. Now the 7-day data: 40, 42, 45, 41, 43, 44, 300. The mean is about 79.3 people, and the median (the 4th value from the smallest) is 43 people.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: If you described the 'typical day' over the 7 days, how would you judge?
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.after: There was not a single day of the 7 with a mean of 79.3 people (the closest days are 45 or 300 people). If you are describing the 'typical day', the median of 43 people is more stable. But it can differ if the purpose is different.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A mean of about 79 people is suitable
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: One festival day pulled the mean up a lot. Look in the data for whether there was actually a day near 79 people.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A median of 43 people is suitable
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This judgment tries to describe the 'typical day' with a value that is less affected by one extreme value.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It depends on what you want to do
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This judgment says that the representative value can differ depending on the purpose it is used for.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 300 people got mixed in, so this data cannot be used
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Just because there is an extreme value, you do not need to throw away all the data. Look at which value is less affected.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: the library expects the next week to also have 7 days including one festival day like this week, and plans to give each visitor 2 information sheets. You want to estimate the total number of sheets needed for the 7 days of next week.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which is the most suitable calculation for estimating the total number of sheets?
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.after: Mean × number of days = the total (79.3×7=555 people). If the purpose is the total amount, the mean is suitable. When describing a typical day, the median can be suitable, and when planning the total amount, the mean can be suitable. Even if you leave your judgment from step 2 (the median) as it is, it is still the right judgment for the purpose of 'typical day'.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Mean of the first 6 days 42.5 people × 7 days × 2 sheets = 595 sheets
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This was calculated with data that leaves out the festival day. Next week will include a festival day.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This was calculated based on a typical day. For the total amount, the many visitors on the festival day are needed too.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Mean about 79.3 people × 7 days × 2 sheets ≈ 1110 sheets
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This judgment uses the fact that mean × number of days is the total of all 7 days.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Largest value 300 people × 7 days × 2 sheets = 4200 sheets
y-m-57-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This assumed that every day is a festival day. You would end up preparing far too many.
y-m-57-06.s.s1.reflect: With the same data, the suitable value changed when the purpose changed. If your judgment changed at step 3, say what changed it, and if it stayed the same, say what purpose you assumed.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.prompt: Give one purpose for which the mean is more suitable and one purpose for which the median is more suitable, and write examples other than a library.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what mean × number of values represents.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.hint.1: When one data value is unusually large, compare using the values from the earlier steps which of the mean and the median moves more.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the reason why the mean is suitable in your example (for example, because the total is needed)?
y-m-57-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: In your example where the median is suitable, did you write specifically what extreme value there is?
y-m-57-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you make a new example that is not about a library?
y-m-57-06.s.s2.model.0: When planning the total cost, the mean is suitable, because mean × number of days is the total. When describing a typical day, the median is more suitable when one or two days are very large.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.model.1: When deciding the total number of trash bags needed for a month, I use the mean, and when describing a typical house price in data like the house prices of one neighborhood that has a few very expensive houses mixed in, the median is better.
y-m-57-06.s.s2.modelNote.1: A model answer written with a different subject

y-m-57-07.title: If two things increase together, are they cause and effect?
y-m-57-07.topic: Relationships in data: scatter plots, correlation and causation
y-m-57-07.goal: Know that a tendency of two variables to change together (correlation) does not mean that one is the cause of the other, judge what evidence and extra data can make you suspect a third factor, and explain it in your own words.
y-m-57-07.material:
This is monthly data for a seaside town. (Water accidents are the number of times the rescue team went out at the town beach.)
January: average temperature 1°C, ice cream sales 10 (thousand), water accidents 0
March: 9°C, 22 (thousand), 1
May: 18°C, 40 (thousand), 2
July: 27°C, 71 (thousand), 5
August: 29°C, 78 (thousand), 6
October: 15°C, 35 (thousand), 1
A friend said, 'If we sell less ice cream, there will be fewer water accidents.'
y-m-57-07.thinking.0: Tell apart what can be read from the table from what cannot
y-m-57-07.thinking.1: Choose extra data to sort out a third factor
y-m-57-07.thinking.2: Rewrite a claim to fit the level of the evidence
y-m-57-07.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-07.prereq.1: Reading the tendency of two variables to grow together (positive correlation) from a table or scatter plot
y-m-57-07.prereq.2: The unit (°C) of values such as the average temperature
y-m-57-07.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable thing to say from this table alone?
y-m-57-07.s.s1.hint.0: Rearrange the table from the month with the smallest sales to the largest and see how the number of accidents changes.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.hint.1: Look for whether the table has data where 'one thing was changed on purpose'.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.o.a: If we reduce sales, the number of accidents will also go down
y-m-57-07.s.s1.r.a: The table has no data where sales were changed on purpose. Changing together is different from changing one and the other changing.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.o.b: In months with high sales, there is a tendency for more accidents too
y-m-57-07.s.s1.r.b: This judgment only states the 'tendency to change together' that can be read from the table.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.o.c: When accidents increase, people buy more ice cream
y-m-57-07.s.s1.r.c: It is the same problem even if you reverse the direction. The table does not show which comes first.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.o.d: There is no relationship at all between sales and the number of accidents
y-m-57-07.s.s1.r.d: In all six months, the higher the sales, the more accidents there were. Read the table again in order.
y-m-57-07.s.s1.explain: What can be read from the table is the tendency (positive correlation) that 'in months with high sales, there are also many accidents'. You cannot say from this alone that one is the cause of the other.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.prompt: What extra data would make the explanation 'it was hot, so ice cream sold more and accidents increased too' more believable?
y-m-57-07.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how the relationship between the two values would have to change in data with the temperature held constant for the explanation 'because of the temperature' to become convincing.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.hint.1: First sort each choice into whether it is 'a comparison with the temperature held the same' or not.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.o.a: In other towns too, sales are highest in July
y-m-57-07.s.s2.r.a: The fact that it is the same in other towns only tells you which months have high sales in this town; it does not tell you whether temperature affects the two values.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.o.b: Even when days with similar temperatures are grouped together, the higher the sales, the more accidents
y-m-57-07.s.s2.r.b: Since the relationship remains even with the temperature held the same, this is data on the side that the temperature alone is not enough to explain it.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.o.c: The month with the most accidents is August
y-m-57-07.s.s2.r.c: This is a fact already in the table. It gives no new information about whether the temperature is the cause.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.o.d: When days with similar temperatures are grouped together, the relationship between the two values becomes weaker
y-m-57-07.s.s2.r.d: If the relationship became weaker once the temperature was held the same, this is a judgment that supports the explanation that the temperature moved both values together.
y-m-57-07.s.s2.explain: If the relationship between the two values becomes weaker when comparing days with the temperature matched, it becomes more likely that the reason the two values moved together was the temperature. On the other hand, if the relationship stays the same even after matching the temperature, that explanation becomes weaker. But that alone does not prove that ice cream is not the cause of the accidents.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.prompt: What would you answer to your friend? Write separately what can be read from the table and what cannot.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.hint.0: Separate the part of your friend's words that talks about 'cause' from the 'tendency' read from the table.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.hint.1: Look in the table for what other element is common to the months in which both values are large.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write specifically the 'what can be read' (the tendency) from the table?
y-m-57-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you make clear what the 'what cannot be read' (the cause) is?
y-m-57-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write what other data or experiment is needed to check that claim?
y-m-57-07.s.s3.model.0: From the table, you can only read the tendency that in months with high sales there are also many accidents. You cannot say for certain that accidents happen because of ice cream, and hot weather may have raised both values. You would have to do an experiment, such as closing the shops, to know.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.model.1: A correlation of increasing together can be seen, but it is not evidence of cause and effect. When the temperature is high, more people visit the beach, so accidents increase and more ice cream sells. So we can't tell whether accidents would go down if we closed the shops.
y-m-57-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that gives the number of visitors as the third factor

y-m-57-08.title: Is the big pizza really more expensive?
y-m-57-08.topic: Similarity of figures: ratio of lengths and ratio of areas
y-m-57-08.goal: Confirm by finding the error in a solution that in similar figures with a given ratio of lengths, the ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of lengths, build sizes that fit a price condition yourself, and state the assumption under which the comparison holds.
y-m-57-08.material: A shop sells pizzas of the same shape (circle) and the same thickness. The small pizza has a diameter of 20cm and costs 12000원, and the large pizza has a diameter of 30cm and costs 24000원. Assume that the amount you can eat is proportional to the area of the pizza. A student explained that 'the large pizza is more expensive for the same amount'.
y-m-57-08.thinking.0: Find the wrong generalization in a line of the solution
y-m-57-08.thinking.1: Build examples that fit a condition using the relationship between the ratio of similarity and the ratio of areas
y-m-57-08.thinking.2: State the assumptions under which the comparison holds and the situations where it breaks
y-m-57-08.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-08.prereq.1: The meaning of similar figures and the ratio of the lengths of corresponding sides (the ratio of similarity)
y-m-57-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in this explanation. (Lines that follow from that line can also be wrong.)
y-m-57-08.s.s1.hint.0: Directly compare the areas of a pizza with a diameter of 10cm and one of 20cm (how many times as large the area is when the length is 2 times).
y-m-57-08.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many squares there are when the side of a square grows from 1 to 2.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.line.0: The diameter of the small pizza is 20cm and the diameter of the large pizza is 30cm.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.line.1: The two pizzas are similar figures and the ratio of similarity is 2:3.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.line.2: For similar figures, the ratio of areas is also the same as the ratio of similarity, so the ratio of areas is 2:3.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.line.3: The area of the large pizza is 1.5 times as large, but the price is 24000÷12000=2 times.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the large pizza is sold at a higher price for the same amount.
y-m-57-08.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right (circles are all similar figures, and the ratio of the diameters is the ratio of similarity). Line 3 is the mistake. If the ratio of similarity is 2:3, the lengths are 2:3, but the ratio of areas is 2×2:3×3=4:9. Lines 4 and 5 are wrong because they use the 1.5 times from line 3 as it is. The area is 2.25 times as large and the price is 2 times, so the large pizza is cheaper for the same amount.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different large pizzas (diameter d cm, price p원) that cost more than the small pizza (diameter 20cm, 12000원) but have a lower price per 1cm². (d and p are integers, 20<d≤40, p≤50000)
y-m-57-08.s.s2.hint.0: First calculate the 'price per one square of the diameter' for the small pizza.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.hint.1: For each candidate (d, p), compare whether p divided by the square of d is less than that standard.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer greater than 20cm and at most 40cm.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The diameter must be an integer greater than 20 and at most 40.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The price is an integer greater than 12000원 and at most 50000원.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The price must be an integer greater than 12000 and at most 50000.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The price per 1cm² is cheaper than the small pizza.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The price per 1cm² is not cheaper than the small pizza.
y-m-57-08.s.s2.explain: The area of a circle is proportional to the square of the diameter, so if the diameter is d, the area is (d/20)² times that of the small pizza. The small pizza is 12000원 per 400 of the square of the diameter, so it is '30원 per one square of the diameter'. So if p÷d² is less than 30, it is cheaper for the same amount. (30, 24000) gives 26.7, (24, 15000) gives 26.0, and (40, 40000) gives 25, all less than 30.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.prompt: For this comparison to hold, what must you assume is the same for the two pizzas? Give and write one situation where that assumption could break.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.hint.0: Think about why only 'area' was used in the comparison, and picture what other than area affects the amount you eat.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how the conclusion would change if that is different between the two pizzas.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain how the assumption you wrote connects to 'the amount you eat is proportional to the area'?
y-m-57-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically how the conclusion changes in the situation where it breaks?
y-m-57-08.s.s3.model.0: You must assume that the thickness and the amount of toppings are the same for the two pizzas. If the middle of the large pizza is thin or has fewer toppings, the amount you eat may not be the same even though the area is larger.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.model.1: I assume both pizzas are round and have the same thickness. If the crust at the edge of the large pizza is thicker, the amount you eat is not proportional to the area, so the conclusion could change.
y-m-57-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that gives the edge crust as the situation

y-m-57-09.title: If the average speed is the same, are they at the same position?
y-m-57-09.topic: Graph of a function: the meaning of average rate of change
y-m-57-09.goal: Know that even if the average speed, the distance traveled divided by time, is the same, the positions in the middle can differ, say what extra information is needed to know the position in the middle, and build pairs of speeds that fit a condition.
y-m-57-09.material: On a straight path in a park, Jiyun and Hajun started at the same place at the same time and walked in the same direction for 20 minutes. Jiyun walked at a steady pace and after 20 minutes arrived at a point 2000m from the starting point. Hajun also arrived at a point 2000m from the starting point after 20 minutes. We do not know how Hajun walked in between. Hajun did not turn back (the direction of movement was always forward or stopped). The unit of speed is m/min.
y-m-57-09.thinking.1: Show with examples that graphs can differ even if the average rate of change is the same
y-m-57-09.thinking.2: Say what extra information is needed
y-m-57-09.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-09.prereq.1: The meaning of speed = distance ÷ time
y-m-57-09.prereq.2: The relationship between distance and time at a constant speed (the graph of a linear function)
y-m-57-09.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable thing to say about the positions of the two people 10 minutes after the start?
y-m-57-09.s.s1.hint.0: First calculate Jiyun's speed and her position after 10 minutes.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.hint.1: Test whether 2000m after 20 minutes is possible even if Hajun walks fast for the first 10 minutes and slowly later.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.r.a: You read the average speed being the same as meaning the positions at every moment are the same. An average only gives one value for the whole interval.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.o.b: Hajun will also be at the 1000m point, because there is no reason to think it is different
y-m-57-09.s.s1.r.b: If you decide they are the same because there is no reason, that becomes an assumption with no basis. They could be the same or different.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.o.c: Hajun must have been ahead of 1000m, because he would have walked harder
y-m-57-09.s.s1.r.c: Who was faster is not in the problem. Tell apart whether your reason comes from the data or is a guess.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.o.d: Jiyun is at the 1000m point, and Hajun's position cannot be decided from this information
y-m-57-09.s.s1.r.d: This judgment says that at a constant speed the position is proportional to time, but we do not know Hajun's movement in between.
y-m-57-09.s.s1.explain: Jiyun's speed is a constant 100m/min, so she is at 1000m after 10 minutes. For Hajun, we only know that the average speed over 20 minutes is 100m/min, and we do not know whether he went fast and then slowed down or went slowly and then sped up. So we cannot decide his position after 10 minutes. To know it, we need more information, such as Hajun's position at the middle time or his speeds in each interval.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.prompt: Suppose Hajun walked the first 10 minutes at a constant speed m1 (m/min) and the last 10 minutes at a constant speed m2 (m/min), and arrived at the 2000m point after 20 minutes. Make 3 different possible (m1, m2) for which he was ahead of Jiyun after 10 minutes. (Write the speed as 0 for an interval where he stopped.)
y-m-57-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write the distance traveled in each of the two intervals, and write as an equation what their sum must be.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.hint.1: Use an inequality to decide what range m1 must be in for the position after 10 minutes to be ahead of 1000m.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.var.m1: Speed in the first 10 minutes m1 (m/min)
y-m-57-09.s.s2.var.m2: Speed in the last 10 minutes m2 (m/min)
y-m-57-09.s.s2.ok.c1: He did not walk backward (the speed is 0 or more).
y-m-57-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The speed must be 0 or more. It was said he did not walk backward.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.ok.c2: He arrived at the 2000m point after 20 minutes.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the distances walked in 20 minutes is not 2000m.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.ok.c3: After 10 minutes he was ahead of Jiyun (1000m).
y-m-57-09.s.s2.fail.c3: The position after 10 minutes (10×m1) is not ahead of Jiyun's 1000m.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.explain: The distance in the first 10 minutes is 10×m1 and the distance in the last 10 minutes is 10×m2, and the sum is 2000m. To be ahead of Jiyun after 10 minutes, 10×m1>1000, that is m1>100, and m2=200−m1. If m1=200, then m2=0 (he stops after 10 minutes) is also possible.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Write one reason why the average speeds of the two people can be the same but their positions after 10 minutes can differ.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the distance Hajun went in the first 10 minutes with the distance Jiyun went in the same time.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think separately about the two people's distances being equal over the whole 20 minutes and their distances being equal at the 10-minute mark.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain the reason using the (m1, m2) you made as an example?
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you make clear which time interval the average speed is a value for?
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The average speed only gives one value for going the whole 20 minutes, so even if he walks fast at first and slowly later, the same average comes out.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.model.1: The average speed is the overall average between the start and the end. If he goes fast for the first 10 minutes and slowly for the last 10 minutes, he can be ahead at the 10-minute mark and still be equal when he arrives.
y-m-57-09.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: A model answer written as a comparison of time points

y-m-57-10.title: On which side is the graph of f(x−2)?
y-m-57-10.topic: Graph of a function: translation and changes in the equation
y-m-57-10.goal: Without depending on the outward look of '−2' in the equation, use the method of checking the position of a graph with function values, and build the equation of a translated parabola that fits a condition yourself.
y-m-57-10.material: You want to move the graph of the function f(x)=x² by some rule to get the graph of g(x)=f(x−2). (On the x-axis, the right is the positive direction.) A student explained the graph of g as below.
y-m-57-10.thinking.0: Verify with values a rule made from the outward look of an equation
y-m-57-10.thinking.1: Find the wrong line and give the reason
y-m-57-10.thinking.2: Build an equation that satisfies a condition yourself and say why one value determines another
y-m-57-10.prereq.0: H2 only shows the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a school grade assignment. Assume that the middle-school level content below has already been learned.
y-m-57-10.prereq.1: Putting a value into a function's equation to find the function value
y-m-57-10.prereq.2: The shape of the graph of y=x² and the fact that its vertex is (0, 0)
y-m-57-10.prereq.3: Putting values into letters and simplifying an expression
y-m-57-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in this explanation. (Lines that follow from that line can also be wrong.)
y-m-57-10.s.s1.hint.0: Put x=2 and x=−2 into g and calculate the values of g.
y-m-57-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare where x makes the value of g smallest with the vertex (0, 0) of f.
y-m-57-10.s.s1.line.0: The vertex of the graph of f(x)=x² is (0, 0).
y-m-57-10.s.s1.line.2: The equation has −2, so the graph was moved by −2 in the x direction, that is, 2 to the left.
y-m-57-10.s.s1.line.3: So the vertex of g is (−2, 0).
y-m-57-10.s.s1.line.4: g(−2)=0, so the vertex is right.
y-m-57-10.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 is the first wrong line. It decided the direction only by the outward look of having −2 in the equation. The x at which g(x)=0 is x=2, when x−2=0, so the vertex is (2, 0) and the graph of f was moved 2 to the right. Lines 4 and 5 follow from line 3, and since g(−2)=(−4)²=16, line 5 is wrong.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.prompt: Consider the parabola y=(x−p)²+q. Make 3 different (p, q) so that this parabola passes through the point (3, 0), and its vertex is to the right (p>0) of the vertex (0, 0) of y=x² and below the x-axis (q<0).
y-m-57-10.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute the coordinates of the point (3, 0) into the equation and write the relationship between p and q in one line.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.hint.1: Choose p, find q, then check the two inequalities p>0 and q<0 each.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.ok.c1: The vertex is to the right of (0, 0).
y-m-57-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The vertex is below the x-axis.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.fail.c3: When you put in x=3, y is not 0.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.explain: Substituting the point (3, 0) gives (3−p)²+q=0, so q=−(3−p)². When p is chosen, q is fixed as one value. If p=3, then q=0, which breaks the condition q<0, so p must be a positive number other than 3. Examples: (4, −1), (5, −4), (2, −1).
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.prompt: Write, with an equation or in words, why choosing p fixes q as one value.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point (3, 0) into x and y of the equation.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.hint.1: Choose one p and find q, then try other p too and look for the rule.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate q yourself for the (p, q) you made?
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why q is 0 or less using a square?
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.model.0: Substituting the point (3,0) gives (3−p)²+q=0, so q=−(3−p)² is fixed as one value. When you choose p, q is determined along with it.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.model.1: Putting in x=3, y=0 gives q as an expression in p, and a square is not negative, so q is always 0 or less. So each p fixes one q.
y-m-57-10.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: A model answer that also explains the sign of q
